specPoints.text: explain that gravitational force: • causes moons to orbit planets • causes the planets to orbit the Sun • causes artificial satellites to orbit the Earth • causes comets to orbit the Sun
describe the differences in the orbits of comets, moons and planets

primer.text: Gravity is the great choreographer: it bends moons around planets, planets around the Sun, satellites around the Earth and comets around the Sun. Planets ride near-circular paths in one plane and slow down with distance; comets loop on hugely stretched ellipses, sprinting past the Sun and drifting on the far leg.

lessons.title: Gravity causes orbits
lessons.opening: Orbital motion happens because of the gravitational attraction between two bodies. That force always points towards the centre of the larger body, and it holds the smaller body on its curved path: moons orbit planets, planets and comets orbit the Sun, and artificial satellites orbit the Earth.
keyPoints: Orbital motion results from gravitational attraction between two bodies.
Gravity's pull on the orbiter always points at the larger body's centre.
Gravity causes moons to orbit planets and planets to orbit the Sun.
Gravity also holds artificial satellites in orbit around the Earth and comets around the Sun.

low.restatement: Gravity aims at the big body's centre, so small bodies keep turning.
low.analogy: A ball on a string swung in a circle: the string tension (gravity) constantly pulls the ball inward, so it circles instead of flying off.
low.examPointer: List all four gravity-caused orbits — moons, planets, satellites, comets — when asked to 'explain that gravitational force causes'.

medium.restatement: Central attraction plus sideways motion equals an orbit: the pull supplies the constant inward turn.
medium.analogy: Whirling a bucket of water: the rope's inward tug is what stops the bucket sailing away in a straight line.
medium.examPointer: Name the larger body's centre as the pull's direction — that 'centre' wording is the mark.

check.stem: What keeps a moon in orbit around its planet?

options.text: the gravitational attraction of the planet
options.explanation: Gravity towards the larger body bends the moon's path into an orbit.
Moons are natural; no engines exist.
Orbits are gravitational, not magnetic.
The planet's pull is what curves the path.

check.stem: In an orbit, the gravitational force on the smaller body points…

options.text: towards the centre of the larger body
options.explanation: The attraction always aims at the larger body's centre.
Attraction pulls inward, never outward.
The force is not along the motion; that is why the path curves.
The dominant pull is from the orbited body.

check.stem: Which pairing of orbiter and orbited body is correct?

options.explanation: The Sun anchors the planetary orbits.
Moons orbit planets.
The larger body is orbited, not the orbiter.
Satellites orbit the Earth.

check.stem: Artificial satellites stay in orbit around the Earth because of…

options.explanation: Gravity supplies the inward force the orbit needs.
Air resistance would drag satellites down.
Speed alone cannot curve the path; force is required.
Solar wind does not hold satellites.

check.stem: Comets travel around…

options.text: the Sun, on stretched elliptical paths
options.explanation: Comets are Sun-orbiters with highly elliptical orbits.
Comets orbit the Sun, not the Earth.
Neither the body nor the shape is right.
The course-level answer is comets orbit the Sun.

check.stem: State what causes orbital motion.
check.modelAnswer: Orbital motion results from the gravitational force of attraction acting between the two bodies.

check.stem: Name the force that keeps satellites in orbit around the Earth.
check.modelAnswer: The Earth's gravitational pull keeps artificial satellites in orbit.

check.stem: Explain why the gravitational force makes an orbiting body move in a circular path.
check.modelAnswer: The pull always points towards the centre of the larger body, so the smaller body is constantly steered inward — a steady inward turn of its motion traces out a circular path.

check.stem: Classify each orbit: our Moon, the planet Neptune, a weather satellite, and Halley's-type comet.
check.modelAnswer: The Moon orbits a planet; Neptune orbits the Sun; the satellite orbits the Earth; the comet orbits the Sun on a highly elliptical path.

lessons.title: Planets and moons in orbit
lessons.opening: Planets share habits: slightly elliptical orbits with the Sun near the centre, all in the same plane, all travelling the same direction — but they differ in radius, speed and period, with distant planets crawling and near planets racing. Moons orbit their planets in circular paths, and the closer the moon, the faster and shorter each orbit.
keyPoints: Planets orbit in slightly elliptical paths, in the same plane and the same direction.
Planets differ in orbital radius, speed and time taken to orbit.
The more distant the planet, the slower its travel and the longer its orbit.
Moons orbit planets in circular paths, faster when closer to the planet.

low.restatement: Planets: same plane, same direction, different radii — distance sets speed.
low.analogy: Runners on a track's outer lanes: the outside runners cover more ground at a jog while inside runners sprint their shorter laps.
low.examPointer: Split the answer into similarities (plane, direction) and differences (radius, speed, period) for full marks.

medium.restatement: Moon orbits are circular and distance-governed: close in means fast, far out means slow.
medium.analogy: Horses on a carousel: the inner horses finish each turn sooner than the outer ones.
medium.examPointer: Keep comet behaviour out of moon answers — circular and regular belong to moons and planets.

check.stem: How do the orbits of the planets compare in direction and plane?

options.text: they all travel the same direction around the Sun, in the same plane
options.explanation: Shared plane and direction are two of the planet similarities.

options.text: each planet picks its own plane and direction
options.explanation: Planets share plane and direction.
The directions are common, not random.
Retrograde motion is not the shared pattern.

check.stem: The further a planet sits from the Sun, the…

options.text: slower it travels and the longer its orbit takes
options.explanation: Distance up, speed down, period up.
Near planets are the fast ones.
Distant planets take longer.
All planetary orbits are slightly elliptical already.

check.stem: A moon orbits its planet in…

options.explanation: Moons follow circular orbits around their planets.

options.text: a highly elliptical path like a comet
options.explanation: That is comet behaviour.

options.text: a straight line past the planet
options.explanation: A straight line is not an orbit.

options.text: an orbit around the Sun instead
options.explanation: Moons orbit planets.

check.stem: Bringing a moon closer to its planet makes its orbit…

options.explanation: Closer moons race round in less time.
That is what distance does, not closeness.
Speed depends on distance.
Orbits do not stand upright like that.

check.stem: Which statement about planetary orbital radii is right?

options.text: planets orbit at different distances from the Sun
options.explanation: Radii differ — that is one of the listed differences.

options.text: all planets share the same orbital radius
options.explanation: Radii differ between planets.

options.text: orbital radius has no effect on speed
options.explanation: Radius sets speed: distant planets are slower.
Orbital radii stay effectively fixed.

check.stem: State the shared features of the planets' orbits.
check.modelAnswer: Their orbits are slightly elliptical with the Sun near the centre, they share one plane, and they travel the same direction.

check.stem: State how a moon's orbit changes as it sits closer to its planet.
check.modelAnswer: The closer moon completes each orbit in less time and at greater speed.

check.stem: Explain why distant planets take longer to orbit the Sun.
check.modelAnswer: The further a planet sits from the Sun, the slower it travels along its orbit, and with a longer path to cover at lower speed each circuit takes more time.

check.stem: Two planets, X near the Sun and Y far out. Compare their orbital speeds and periods.
check.modelAnswer: Planet X, nearer the Sun, travels faster and completes each orbit sooner; planet Y travels more slowly and takes longer for each circuit.

lessons.title: Comet orbits
lessons.opening: Comets break the planetary pattern: their orbits are highly elliptical or hyperbolic, they need not share the planets' plane or direction, and their speed swings wildly — increasing as they approach the Sun and decreasing as they recede.
keyPoints: Comet orbits are highly elliptical or hyperbolic.
A comet's speed changes a lot as its distance from the Sun changes.
Comets need not orbit in the planets' plane, and some travel the opposite direction.
Comets speed up as they approach the Sun and slow down as they move away.

low.restatement: Comets: stretched orbits, wild speed swings — fast near the Sun, slow far away.
low.analogy: A skateboarder in a half-pipe: fastest at the bottom (near the Sun), crawling at the rims (far away).
low.examPointer: 'Highly elliptical' is the phrase to quote; 'stretched circle' glosses it nicely in explanations.

medium.restatement: Speed and distance trade against each other along the comet's ellipse: closest approach is the fastest point.
medium.analogy: A bicycle descending a valley and climbing the far side: speed builds on the descent, drains on the climb.
medium.examPointer: Direction-of-travel questions: match 'approaching' with speeding up and 'receding' with slowing down.

check.stem: The shape of a comet's orbit is…

options.explanation: Stretched ellipses and hyperbolas are comet territory.
Comet orbits are strongly stretched.
No orbit is square.
Comet orbits differ sharply from planetary ones.

check.stem: As a comet approaches the Sun, its speed…

options.explanation: Approach means speed-up; recession means slow-down.
Comet speed changes with distance.
That happens on the outward leg.

options.text: drops to zero at closest approach
options.explanation: Closest approach is the fastest point.

check.stem: As a comet moves away from the Sun, its speed…

options.explanation: Distance gained is speed lost.
The speed-up belongs to the approach.
Speed varies along the orbit.
Speed has nothing to do with shape here.

check.stem: Comet orbits compared with planetary orbits…

options.text: need not share the planets' plane and may run the opposite direction
options.explanation: Inclination and direction are not fixed for comets.

options.text: always lie in the planets' plane
options.explanation: Comets are not confined to that plane.

options.text: always run the same direction as planets
options.explanation: Some comets run counter to the planets.

options.text: never pass close to the Sun
options.explanation: Close approaches are the hallmark of comet orbits.

check.stem: Why does a comet's speed change significantly along its orbit?

options.text: its distance from the Sun changes dramatically on the stretched orbit
options.explanation: Large distance swings drive large speed swings.
Comets have no engines.

options.text: because the Sun's gravity vanishes far away
options.explanation: Gravity weakens with distance but never vanishes.
Collisions are not part of the orbital story.

check.stem: Describe the shape of a comet's orbit.
check.modelAnswer: A comet's orbit is highly elliptical — very stretched — or hyperbolic.

check.stem: State how a comet's speed changes during one orbit.
check.modelAnswer: The comet speeds up as it approaches the Sun and slows down as it moves away.

check.stem: Explain why comet orbits differ so much from planetary orbits.
check.modelAnswer: Comets follow highly elliptical or hyperbolic paths rather than the planets' near-circular, single-plane circles, so their distance from the Sun — and hence their speed — swings enormously, and their planes and directions need not match the planets'.

check.stem: A comet is observed slowing down over successive nights. State where it is in its orbit relative to the Sun.
check.modelAnswer: The comet is moving away from the Sun on the outward leg of its orbit, where its speed decreases.

glossary.definition: The attraction between bodies that steers orbiters around the larger body's centre.
A stretched-circle orbit; comets follow highly elliptical or hyperbolic paths.
How fast an orbiter moves; planets slow with distance, comets swing with theirs.
